title: The Nature of the Law
summary: The opening part argues that death is an enemy whose “chauffeur” is the law, so freedom from the law is freedom from death. The series defines “the law” broadly: the law of Moses plus the “elementary principles of the world” (cause-and-effect formulas such as “70 years equals death”). It traces the law’s origin to Eden (trying to become what you already are) and to Sinai, where, it claims, Israel refused God’s grant covenant and demanded a treaty-style covenant, so it is called the law of Moses rather than the law of God. The law’s purpose was to magnify humanity’s distorted form, not to make anyone righteous, and legalism and life cannot coexist. Comparing 2 Cor 3, the glory of the old covenant is death and condemnation, while the new covenant’s glory is the Spirit, life and righteousness, displayed at the transfiguration.
thesis: The law, meaning both the Mosaic code and the world’s performance-based formulas, is the vehicle of death, so stepping fully out of law and striving into Christ’s finished work is the doorway to life and immortality.

flow.text: Death is an enemy and the law is what delivers it; remove the law and death has no way to arrive. The law brought death and wrath.
The Bible’s “law” covers the law of Moses and the elementary principles of the world. Deliverance from both is presented as the path to immortality.
John 1 gives the spiritual view of creation and Genesis the natural one. Moses, who wrote Genesis by revelation, showed that grasping to become like God brings death.

flow.step: No striving in the finished work
flow.text: A personal story shows that Christ’s finished work cannot be improved on, only stepped into. Life is governed from the spirit inward, not by senses or visible evidence.
Only humans were given authority to redeem creation, and God would not override that grant. If losing your body means losing dominion, death cannot be part of God’s plan.
Heb 11 shows the departed are still waiting for perfection, which comes by resurrection. You enter what God gave before the world began by believing, not by earning.
Paul fought legalism fiercely because life and immortality, given before time and revealed in the gospel, can only be stepped into, never earned.

flow.step: Origin of the law at Sinai
flow.text: God offered a grace covenant with no laws beyond Passover and Sabbath, and a priestly calling for all Israel. Israel, used to Egyptian covenant forms, demanded a different covenant.

Ancient kings made mutual treaties, kept two copies in an ark and swore to be punishable by their gods. God, having no one higher, let Israel keep both copies, and they effectively asked to be punished if they broke it.
The law confined, condemned and aroused sin, magnifying humanity’s distortion so it could be seen and fixed. It proved people were not like God rather than making them so.
Jesus warned that any legalism blocks the kingdom; the disciples, worrying about bread after two miracle feedings, showed life-giving spirits ruled by circumstances.
A new covenant requires a new priesthood, sacrifice and temple; Paul wrote in the transitional period between the cross and AD 70.
Glory (doxa) means the opinion or reputation of something: the law’s glory is death and condemnation, the Spirit’s glory is life and righteousness.
Moses’ face was veiled after receiving the law; Jesus was transfigured by the Spirit of life while the Law and Prophets looked on, and the Father said to listen to Him.

teachings.title: The law is death’s chauffeur
teachings.body: Death is an enemy, and the law is what brings it to us. The series reasons that if the vehicle is removed, the enemy does not show up. The law is said to bring wrath, which the sermon glosses as making a person fit for wrath.

teachings.title: Law means more than the Mosaic code
teachings.body: The Bible uses “law” for two things: the law of Moses, which was given to Israel and condemned them, and the elementary principles of the world. Being delivered from both is presented as the route to immortality.

teachings.title: The elementary principles of the world
teachings.body: The sermon says kosmos means an ordered or contractual arrangement. Its “elements” are formulas of cause and effect, such as one plus one equals two, fifty years of work equals retirement, and seventy years equals death. To step away from death you must step away from these formulas.

teachings.title: Poor covenant understanding means dying by faith
teachings.body: If believers are not freed from wrong ideas about covenant, they will keep dying while trusting God. Humans did not lose their dominion in the fall; they lost their identity, and they lost it through the law.

teachings.title: John 1 as the spiritual view of creation
teachings.body: Genesis 1 gives creation from the natural side and John 1 from the spiritual side. The series says John was correcting the Genesis account when he contrasted the law given through Moses with grace and truth through Jesus.

teachings.title: Moses saw God’s glory as creation
teachings.body: After Moses spoke with God face to face, he asked to see God’s glory and was hidden in the rock and shown God’s back, which the sermon says is not a crude image. Moses was hidden in the Word, in Christ, and was shown creation “in the beginning”, which became Genesis by divine revelation.

teachings.title: How the law came through Moses
teachings.body: Without Moses’ account we would not know humanity had a destiny before the fall that was not ruled by the senses. Genesis 1–3 shows that trying to do something to become like God brings death. The tree of knowledge killed humanity, not because of the fruit itself, but because of the heart posture needed to want it.

teachings.title: A man as both power and love
teachings.body: As a marriage aside, a man is a blend of power and love, like Lord and Savior. Power without love eventually turns aggression on the wife. Love without power is good intentions without follow-through: a knight rather than a king, doing what she says instead of what she needs.

teachings.title: No striving in the finished work
teachings.body: Christ’s finished work cannot be improved on; you either step into it or stay out. Life in Christ does not look for visible evidence. God’s Spirit testifies to your spirit first, not to your senses or intellect, and governance from within is the key to life.

teachings.title: The body as the garment, the person as a life-giving spirit
teachings.body: The mortal body is like the garment the woman with the issue of blood touched. The person is the life-giving spirit that gives the garment contact with a creation that needs redeeming, and the Spirit gives life to the mortal body.

teachings.title: Only humans can redeem creation
teachings.body: Humans are the only species given authority to redeem the earth. God did not stop Eve because stepping in would break His own grant of dominion, and then He could never be trusted. For about 4,000 years God worked only through human beings, on earth as in heaven.

teachings.title: Death is not part of the plan
teachings.body: If you lose your body you lose your dominion. If God means creation to be redeemed by humans who look like Him, death cannot be part of His plan.

teachings.title: Death does not bring perfection
teachings.body: Heb 11 lists people who died, and the series calls it a record of their longing. They will not be made perfect without us, so the departed are still waiting for perfection, which lies in resurrection. The sermon says believing that death perfects you makes the cross needless and is unbiblical.

teachings.title: Believe you already are
teachings.body: What God gave before the foundation of the world cannot be entered by earning, striving, trying or deserving, only by believing you already are it. Trusting senses, experience or effort to get there will kill you. Adam and Eve died reaching for what was already theirs.

teachings.title: Why Paul opposed the law so fiercely
teachings.body: Paul fought the law because he knew what it did, and the sermon calls him an immortal. He wished those who pushed circumcision would cut themselves off, and he cursed even angels preaching another gospel. The sermon applies this as refusing anyone who offers death as a savior.

teachings.title: Paul’s gospel: life and immortality already given
teachings.body: Paul aimed to bring life and immortality but spent most of his effort tearing down legalism. Under either the elementary principles or the Mosaic law, people keep striving and dying. God gave life and immortality before time began and revealed them in Christ through the gospel, so believers lack nothing.

teachings.title: Reaching out your hand kills you
teachings.body: The moment you think you must eat something, follow a rule, read a book or attend somewhere to become something, you die. The local church is the hope of the world, but attending does not make you immortal; your new nature draws you to it.

teachings.title: Law of Moses, not law of God
teachings.body: The series says Scripture calls it the law of Moses and that it came through Moses, not from God. Read carefully, as a Berean would, Exodus 19 shows God did not desire the law.

teachings.title: God’s original grant covenant at Sinai
teachings.body: God gives only one kind of covenant, a royal grant in which the greater blesses the lesser. He invited all Israel up the mountain, promised to be their God and to send hornets to drive out their enemies, and gave no laws. The only two commands after Egypt were to keep Passover and Sabbath, meaning life and rest.

teachings.title: A kingdom of priests to reconcile all
teachings.body: God called all Israel to be priests, and priests reconcile humanity to God. If Israel had listened there would have been no enemies, only peoples moved by hornets and reconciled by priests. God never wanted to shut out parts of humanity and never desired to judge anyone.

teachings.title: “God is love but also wrath” is not in the Bible
teachings.body: The series says Scripture never pairs love and wrath this way. God is faithful, so He keeps His promises even when what He promised runs against His character, which explains how wrath came in.

teachings.title: Israel demanded a different covenant
teachings.body: God offered a covenant of blessing with no laws, if they would come up the mountain. Former slaves knew only Pharaoh’s covenants between equals, so they reduced God to their own understanding and demanded a different deal. The sermon says the law of God was rejected and the law of Moses was demanded.

teachings.title: Treaty practice behind the ark
teachings.body: In ancient treaties between kings, each party kept a copy, put it in a box at its god’s temple and swore to be punishable by that god if unfaithful. The sermon presents this as the root of “I swear to God”. The box was an ark, and the sermon says these sacred furnishings existed among pagans before Israel.

teachings.title: Israel asked to be punished
teachings.body: Israel promised to keep the commandments, which the sermon numbers at 619. Swearing by no one greater than Himself, God let them keep both copies, so Israel effectively asked God to punish them if they broke it. God used that season to lead humanity to life by showing that the law cannot give life.

teachings.title: Death reigned before the law; the law highlighted it
teachings.body: Death reigned from Adam to Moses before the commandment, and the law was added to make sin visible. Paul says the law confined him under sin, condemned his conscience and stirred up his sin nature; he would not have coveted if it had not forbidden it. It amplified humanity’s distorted form so it could be fixed.

teachings.title: The law proved we were not like God
teachings.body: The law exposed sin, meaning distorted humanity, so people would know they were made for something better. It was not a righteous requirement to make you more like God; it showed that you were not.

teachings.title: Legalism and life cannot coexist
teachings.body: Any legalism left in a believer is where they will be talked out of life and identity. Jesus warned that the Pharisees’ leaven, their doctrine, keeps people from the kingdom.

teachings.title: Ministry of death vs ministry of the Spirit
teachings.body: Paul calls the covenant engraved on stone a ministry of death and condemnation. The ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness far outshines it, so that the old glory has no glory by comparison.

teachings.title: Post promises, not commandments
teachings.body: The sermon supports removing the Ten Commandments from schools because the commandments killed people. It suggests posting new-covenant promises instead: you are as He is, more than a conqueror, blameless, holy, perfect and a redeemer of creation. Everything the law demanded, Jesus gave.

teachings.title: Covenant change requires three replacements
teachings.body: As a key to interpretation, the series says a covenant change must replace the priesthood, the temple and the sacrifice. Jesus ended sacrifice and offering. John the Baptist, a priest by descent from Aaron, washed the new Melchizedek priest in the Jordan. The temple fell in AD 70.

teachings.title: Paul wrote in a transition
teachings.body: Paul’s letters fall roughly between AD 33 and 70, a 40-year period when the old covenant was fading and the new creation was being planted. That is why he speaks of something passing away.

teachings.title: Glory as reputation
teachings.body: Doxa, the sermon says, has no content of its own and means the opinion held of its subject. The law’s glory is death and condemnation, while the Spirit’s greater glory is life and righteousness.

teachings.title: Moses’ veil vs Jesus’ transfiguration
teachings.body: Moses came down carrying the law’s glory and had to veil his face, the sermon says, because people saw death and condemnation in it. Jesus was transfigured by the law of the Spirit of life, with divinity embodied in humanity, while the Law and Prophets watched. God told Peter to listen to His Son: truth came through Jesus, the law through Moses.

stories.title: Moses and God’s “back”
stories.text: Having spoken with God as a friend, Moses asked to see His glory and was shown God’s back. The preacher jokes that this cannot be crude unless God’s back were more glorious than His face. His point is that God hid Moses in the Word and showed him creation, which became Genesis.

stories.title: “It’s getting better” — the marriage lesson
stories.text: Early in marriage the pastor wanted to be the rescuer of a wife who had suffered abuse, and he became passive. A friend asked how his masculinity was coming, and when he said it was getting better, the friend said that was exactly the problem. Christ’s finished work cannot be improved on, only stepped into.

stories.title: Why God didn’t stop Eve
stories.text: Had God stepped in at the tree, He would have broken His own word giving humans dominion, and He could never be trusted again. So God works His will only through human beings.

stories.title: Paul and the legalists
stories.text: In a deliberately shocking aside, the preacher notes that Paul wished the circumcision party would cut themselves off and cursed even angels preaching another gospel. The application is to reject any message that offers death as a savior.

stories.title: The treaty demonstration with two volunteers
stories.text: Two volunteers play kings of different nations who sign a mutual-defense treaty. Because they serve different gods, each puts a copy in a box at his own temple and swears to be punished by his god if unfaithful. The preacher uses this to explain the two tablets and the ark, and why God handed Israel both copies.

stories.title: The children’s book about a dragon
stories.text: In a picture book a psychologist often cites, a boy blames the mess on a dragon while his mother insists dragons do not exist. The dragon grows until it walks off with the house, and only then is it acknowledged; it grew because it wanted to be noticed. Likewise the law amplified sin so humanity would notice the problem.

stories.title: The disciples and the bread
stories.text: When Jesus warned about the Pharisees’ leaven, the disciples thought He was upset they had forgotten bread. The preacher reads it as Jesus rebuking life-giving spirits who had just seen miracle feedings yet worried about resources. Legalism means being ruled by outward circumstances.

stories.title: Ten Commandments in schools
stories.text: The pastor once got in trouble for saying he supports removing the Ten Commandments from schools. If children must be told not to kill at school, he says, the parenting has failed. He suggests posting gospel promises instead, which most people would not even recognize as religious.

stories.title: Two transfigurations
stories.text: Moses’ face shone with the law’s glory, so he veiled it and people avoided him. Jesus shone with the Spirit’s glory on the mountain, and God told Peter not to build three tents but to listen to His Son. The contrast is death and condemnation versus life and righteousness.

words.claimed: To make someone fit for something; the law fits you for wrath.
words.lexicon: To achieve, accomplish, produce or bring about (BDAG); in a few places it means to prepare someone for something (2 Cor 5:5). In Rom 4:15 the law produces wrath.

words.claimed: An orderly agreement or contractual arrangement.
words.lexicon: Order or arrangement, adornment, the world or universe, humanity, or the world system opposed to God (BDAG/LSJ). It never means a contract.

words.word: stoicheia tou kosmou (“elementary principles of the world”)
words.claimed: Life’s cause-and-effect formulas, such as 70 years equals death.
words.lexicon: Basic elements, rudiments or first principles, or elemental spirits or powers (BDAG; scholars debate the sense in Gal 4 and Col 2). The application to ordinary life formulas is the sermon’s own.

words.claimed: It has no meaning of its own and means the opinion held of its subject; the law’s glory is death.
words.lexicon: In classical Greek: opinion, expectation or reputation. In the LXX and NT, mainly glory, splendor, brightness and honor (translating Hebrew kavod). In 2 Cor 3:7 it is the visible radiance of Moses’ face.

words.claimed: God’s “hinder parts” is not a crude image.
words.lexicon: Back side or rear, also used for “after” or “behind”; in context, the after-effects of God’s passing presence.

questions.q: What two things does the series include in “the law”, and why does it matter?
questions.a: The law of Moses and the elementary principles of the world, the cause-and-effect formulas people live by, such as “seventy years equals death”. Both bring death, so the series holds that freedom from both, not just from Mosaic rules, opens the way to life and immortality.

questions.q: Why does the sermon say it is called the law of Moses rather than the law of God?
questions.a: God offered a grace covenant with no laws except Passover and Sabbath. Israel, knowing only Egyptian treaty covenants, demanded a deal between equals, so the law came through Moses at the people’s demand rather than from God’s desire.

questions.q: What does the ancient treaty-box practice reveal about the two tablets?
questions.a: Treaty partners each kept a copy in a box at their god’s temple and swore to be punished if unfaithful. Because God has no one greater to swear by, He gave Israel both copies, so by their own covenant Israel was asking God to punish them for breaking it.

questions.q: If the law could not make anyone righteous, why was it given?
questions.a: To make sin, humanity’s distorted form, so visible that people would see they were made for more, like the dragon that grew until it was noticed. It confined, condemned and aroused sin, proving people were unlike God rather than making them like Him.

questions.q: How did the Eden story show the law at work before Sinai?
questions.a: Adam and Eve reached to become like God when they already were. The heart posture of grasping, not the fruit itself, brought death, so whenever we try to earn what we already have, we die.

questions.q: What is the difference between the glory on Moses’ face and the glory at the transfiguration?
questions.a: Glory is the opinion held of a thing. Moses carried the law’s glory, death and condemnation, so he had to veil it. Jesus shone with the Spirit’s glory, life and righteousness, and the Father told the disciples to listen to Him.

questions.q: What did the friend’s “that’s your problem” teach about the finished work?
questions.a: Christ’s work cannot be improved by gradual effort; you step into it or stay out. Looking for visible progress is still living by the senses instead of by the Spirit’s witness within.

practice: Notice and drop any trace of legalism, the earning, striving, trying and deserving through which you get talked out of life and identity.
Question life formulas like “seventy years equals death” or “retirement at fifty” instead of living under them.
Stop measuring life in Christ by visible evidence or progress; trust the Spirit’s inner witness that you are a son.
Believe you already are what God made you before time began, rather than reaching to become it.
Go to the local church because your nature draws you there, not as a performance that earns life.
In marriage, men should hold power and love together: protecting while loving, leading by what she needs, not only what she says.
Replace commandment-based identity with new-covenant promises: blameless, holy, more than a conqueror.

fair.claim: Being delivered from the law and the world’s formulas makes believers immortal, so they need not physically die.
fair.note: Mainstream Christian teaching holds that believers still die physically, apart from those alive at Christ’s return, and that immortality is put on at the resurrection. Scripture describes Christian deaths as “falling asleep” and being with Christ. Paul himself, called “an immortal” in the sermon, expected his death. Charitable reading: Christ has defeated death’s sting and its power to hold or terrify believers, and eternal life begins now (John 11:25–26).

fair.claim: The Bible calls it the law of Moses, never the law of God, and God never desired it.
fair.note: Factually wrong as stated. Scripture often calls the Sinai law the law of God or of the Lord: Nehemiah calls it God’s law given by Moses, the Psalms praise the law of the Lord as perfect, and Paul delights in the law of God and calls it holy, just and good. Jesus said He came to fulfil the law, not to abolish it. Charitable reading: the New Testament contrasts Moses and Christ as covenant mediators (John 1:17; Heb 3:1–6), and the law was temporary, a guardian until Christ (Gal 3:19–25).

fair.claim: At Sinai God offered a grace covenant with no laws, and Israel demanded a law covenant instead.
fair.note: Exod 19:5–6 already makes the offer conditional (“if you obey my voice and keep my covenant”), and the Decalogue is spoken by God Himself (Exod 20:1). Most scholars read Sinai as God’s own suzerain-vassal treaty, while royal grants describe the covenants with Abraham and David. The sermon also uses the terms loosely: it calls God’s offer both a “royal grant” and a “suzerain-vassal covenant”, and a treaty between equals is a parity treaty, not a “kinship covenant”. Israel did ask Moses, rather than God, to speak to them (Exod 20:18–19; Deut 5:23–28), which is the strongest support for the reading. The hornet promise (Exod 23:28) is part of the law code, not a law-free offer.

fair.claim: The ark and tabernacle furnishings were “Roman” before they were Israelite; “I swear to God” comes from treaty practice; there are 619 commandments.
fair.note: Rome did not exist in Moses’ time (traditionally founded 753 BC), so this is an anachronism. The real background is second-millennium BC Hittite and Egyptian treaties, which were stored in temples, and some scholars, following Meredith Kline, think the two tablets were duplicate treaty copies. The oath-phrase origin is speculative. Rabbinic tradition counts 613 commandments, not 619. Charitable reading: “Roman” stands loosely for pagan or ancient Near Eastern practice.

fair.claim: “God is love, but He is also wrath” is not in the Bible, and God never desired to judge anyone.
fair.note: Scripture often speaks of God’s wrath and judgment, and Paul tells readers to consider both God’s kindness and His severity. Jesus is appointed judge. Charitable reading: “God is love” describes His essence (1 John 4:8), while wrath is His opposition to evil rather than a second, equal attribute. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11).

fair.claim: The law was not a righteous requirement; it only proved we were not like God.
fair.note: Paul explicitly speaks of the “righteous requirement of the law” being fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit, and calls the law holy and spiritual. Part 2 of the series itself mentions a righteous requirement that needed satisfying. Charitable reading: the law could not give righteousness or life (Gal 3:21; Rom 3:20), which is Paul’s real point.

fair.claim: John was correcting what Moses wrote in Genesis.
fair.note: John 1 deliberately echoes Gen 1 (“In the beginning”) to show Christ as the Creator Word; it neither corrects nor contradicts it. Jesus affirmed that Moses wrote about Him. Charitable reading: John 1 gives a fuller, Christ-centred view of creation.

fair.claim: When Moses asked to see God’s glory, God showed him creation, and this became Genesis.
fair.note: This is speculative. The text says God made His goodness pass by and proclaimed His name: merciful, gracious and slow to anger, but not leaving the guilty unpunished. Moses’ authorship of Genesis is traditional, but the text does not link it to Exod 33. (The transcript says “Jesus” spoke face to face with God, an evident slip for Moses.)

fair.claim: God cannot intervene in human affairs without breaking His word of dominion, so His will was “written out” of history for 4,000 years.
fair.note: Scripture shows God acting sovereignly throughout the Old Testament: the flood, the call of Abraham, the plagues and the Red Sea. He rules over human kingdoms and directs history even through human sin. Charitable reading: God chose to work through human partners and finally through the incarnate Son, the true human (Heb 2:6–9).

fair.claim: Hebrews 11 records the jealousy of those who died, and believing death brings perfection makes Christ’s cross needless.
fair.note: Heb 11 presents these people as heroes of faith who “died in faith” and are commended, not as jealous. Heb 12:23 speaks of “the spirits of the righteous made perfect” in heaven. Charitable reading: Heb 11:39–40 does say final perfection, the resurrection, awaits all God’s people together, so death is not the goal.

fair.claim: Paul hated the law, and wished legalists castrated in Galatians 3.
fair.note: Paul opposed using the law as a way to be justified, but he upheld the law as holy and said faith establishes it. The “cut themselves off” remark is Gal 5:12, not Gal 3, and the curse on any messenger, even an angel, is Gal 1:8–9. Charitable reading: Paul’s anger was against forcing Gentiles under the law as a condition of salvation.

fair.claim: Moses veiled his face because people saw death and condemnation in it.
fair.note: Exodus says Moses’ face shone because he had been speaking with God. The people were afraid, and he wore a veil when not speaking with God. Paul says the veil kept Israel from seeing the end of a glory that was fading. The sermon’s point that the old covenant was a ministry of death is Pauline (2 Cor 3:7), but its explanation of the veil goes beyond the text.

fair.claim: Details of the transfiguration: Enoch and Elijah appeared; God said “those are My sons”; people came from surrounding cities.
fair.note: Factual slips: Moses and Elijah appeared; the voice said “This is My beloved Son” (singular); and only Peter, James and John were present. The point that the Father exalted Jesus above the Law and the Prophets is faithful to the text.

fair.claim: John the Baptist, as a priest, consecrated Jesus as the new Melchizedekian priest at baptism, and the old covenant fully expired only in AD 70.
fair.note: John’s priestly lineage is biblical (Luke 1:5). Reading Jesus’ baptism as a priestly ordination is a minority view, since the Gospels present it as anointing, identification and fulfilling all righteousness. Hebrews places Christ’s priesthood in His offering and exaltation. Many scholars accept a transitional period up to AD 70 (Heb 8:13), but the new covenant is usually dated from the cross.

fair.claim: Humans lost identity, not dominion; only humans can redeem creation and God “can’t”.
fair.note: Debated. Hebrews says we do not yet see everything subject to humanity but we do see Jesus, which points to a loss of dominion that is restored in Christ. Redemption is presented as God’s own work in Christ. Charitable reading: God redeems through the incarnate Man, and believers share in His mission.

fair.claim: The disciples-and-bread episode: Jesus called them idiots and warned that any legalism keeps you out of the kingdom.
fair.note: Jesus rebuked them as “you of little faith” for not understanding, and the warning was about the Pharisees’ and Sadducees’ (or Herod’s) teaching; the text does not mention losing the kingdom. The sermon also mixes up the 4,000 and 5,000 feedings. Charitable reading: it rightly notes that the disciples, focused on bread, missed Jesus’ provision and His warning about false teaching.

fair.claim: The children’s book is cited by a different title.
fair.note: The story described matches Jack Kent’s “There’s No Such Thing as a Dragon” (1975). The illustration and its point stand.
